TERRAFORM PLAN BLAST RADIUS CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Which of these resources is your terraform apply about to destroy?

Paste or load a Terraform structured plan (terraform show -json) and get a deterministic blast-radius report: every destroy and replace called out individually with the attribute that forced it, grouped counts by resource type and by module, and a loud flag when a replace lands on something that holds data.

Nothing is uploaded. The file you load is read in this browser and never leaves your device — which matters here, because a structured plan describes your whole infrastructure.

1. Load your plan

2. What this apply takes away

Every destroy and replace, most consequential first

AddressActionTypeModuleForced byReason

By resource type

TypeCreateUpdateReplaceDestroyNo-op

By module

ModuleCreateUpdateReplaceDestroyNo-op

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a gate before you apply?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file — run it right after you generate the plan, before anything applies it:

terraform plan -out=tfplan && terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json
node cli.mjs check plan.json                            # exit 1 if a replace hits something that holds data
node cli.mjs check plan.json --fail-on=delete-stateful  # also fail on destroying stored data outright
node cli.mjs check plan.json --fail-on=destructive      # fail on any destroy or replace at all
node cli.mjs check plan.json --json

The default gate is replace-stateful rather than "any destroy" on purpose: a gate that fires on every plan in a repository that uses count is one somebody adds continue-on-error to within a week.

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. It reads only the local file you name: no network call, ever.

Which resource types count as holding data

The heuristic is on the type name, split on underscores and matched against a token list per category. What each category stands to lose:

CategoryWhat a replace costs youExample type tokens

Configuration sub-resources are exempt by suffix — aws_db_parameter_group and aws_s3_bucket_policy carry a stateful token and hold no data of their own. The full reasoning, and the upstream issue that makes this worth a separate tool: why a Terraform replace destroys data, and why the plan does not always tell you which attribute forced it. Already have Sentinel or OPA? see how this checker compares to writing your own policy. Worried about the other thing a plan file exposes? Terraform Plan Secret Exposure Check reads the same file for a different failure — attribute values that look like real secrets which the provider schema never marked sensitive. Want to know what the same plan costs rather than what it destroys? Terraform Plan Cost Estimate prices it per month.

Common questions

Why can't I just read the Plan: N to add, N to change, N to destroy line?

Because a replacement is counted in both the add column and the destroy column, so that line cannot tell you whether the 2 destroys are a pair of scratch resources going away or your production database being recreated empty. The detail that separates them is hundreds of lines further up, in a diff nobody scrolls back through. This tool reads the same plan and puts the replaces and destroys at the top, each with the attribute that forced it.

How does it decide a resource type holds data?

By the resource type name, split on underscores and matched against a token list per category — database, disk or volume, bucket, DNS, load balancer, secret, stateful Kubernetes object, queue or stream, and search cluster. Type names are the one part of a plan that is stable across providers and needs no schema lookup, so this works offline against a provider the tool has never seen. It is deliberately biased toward flagging, because an extra flag costs five seconds of reading and a missed one costs a database, and the report always names the token that matched so you can dismiss a false positive at a glance.

Is my plan uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses a pasted or locally loaded file entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads only a local file — no network call, ever. That matters more than usual here: a structured plan contains your whole infrastructure layout and often real attribute values.

What file does it need?

The structured plan JSON from terraform show -json, not the human-readable terraform plan output and not the line-by-line terraform plan -json stream. Run: terraform plan -out=tfplan && terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json

Why is a replace sometimes listed with no attribute that forced it?

Because the plan did not carry one. replace_paths is populated when a provider marks the change as requiring replacement, but a resource replaced because it is tainted or because you passed -replace=ADDRESS has no forcing attribute at all. In those cases the tool shows the action_reason code instead, which is what the plan does say.

Does a clean report mean the apply is safe?

No. It means nothing in this plan matched the patterns this tool checks. It cannot know that a resource you consider disposable is actually load-bearing, it does not read your state file or your provider's source, and it makes no judgement about the change itself. Read the plan before you apply it — this is one gate, not a guarantee.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is informational only — it is not legal, financial, security, compliance, or other professional advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional, your provider's documentation, or your own review of the plan. It reports a deterministic reading of the plan file you supplied and a name-based heuristic for which resource types hold data; it cannot prove an apply is safe, only report what it matched. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output, and for reading the real plan, before you apply anything. vs-writing-your-own-sentinel-opa-policy..text:
← Terraform Plan Blast Radius Check

This checker vs. writing your own Sentinel or OPA policy

Same failure, different cost. Sentinel and OPA/Conftest can both stop an apply that destroys or replaces a stateful resource — once somebody writes and maintains a policy that says which resource types count. This tool ships that detection already built, with no policy language and no platform to adopt.

What each one is for

Sentinel is HashiCorp's policy-as-code engine, bundled with Terraform Cloud and Terraform Enterprise. OPA (Open Policy Agent) and Conftest are open-source alternatives that evaluate a plan against a policy written in Rego, usually wired into CI by hand. Both are general-purpose: an organization typically uses them for cost ceilings, region allow-lists, tagging rules, module version pins, and destructive-change checks, all as separate policies someone writes, reviews, and keeps current as providers add resource types.

This tool checks exactly one thing — whether a replace or destroy in the plan lands on a resource type that holds data — and ships that detection already built, as a zero-dependency Node.js CLI or a browser page that reads the same terraform show -json file. There is no policy to author, no Rego or Sentinel language to learn, and no Terraform Cloud or Enterprise subscription to adopt just to get this one check.

It exists because that one check is easy to write once and easy to let go stale. See why a replace destroys data, and why the plan text does not always say which attribute forced it for the mechanics this tool's token-matching heuristic is built against.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Is this apply about to destroy a database, disk, or bucket, right now?This checker — paste or load your plan, free, no account.
Do I already have a Sentinel or OPA policy for this?Check its resource-type list against this checker's report; a name-based heuristic catches types a hand-written list has not been updated for yet.
Do I need to buy Terraform Cloud/Enterprise for policy-as-code?Only if you want Sentinel specifically, or its other policy features. This one check needs no platform.
Should I replace my whole Sentinel/OPA policy set with this?No — those cover cost, tagging, region, and version rules this tool does not attempt. Run this alongside them for the destroy/replace question.
Is my plan uploaded anywhere?No. The browser page and the CLI both read the file locally and make no network call.

This checker is a narrow, zero-configuration alternative to one specific policy, not a policy-as-code platform. It does not evaluate cost, tagging, region, or version rules, and it does not integrate with Terraform Cloud's or Terraform Enterprise's policy sets.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: the CLI reads a local file with no network call, and the browser page parses a pasted or loaded file entirely on your device.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or write a Sentinel or OPA policy instead?

They solve the same problem at different costs. Sentinel (bundled with Terraform Cloud/Enterprise) and OPA/Conftest can both block an apply that would destroy or replace a stateful resource — once somebody writes a policy in Sentinel's or Rego's policy language that enumerates which resource types count as stateful, keeps that list current as your providers add types, and maintains it across every workspace. This tool ships that detection already built, as a plain Node.js CLI or a browser page, with nothing to write and nothing to keep in sync.

Do I need Terraform Cloud or Enterprise to use this?

No. Sentinel policies only run inside Terraform Cloud or Terraform Enterprise, so adopting Sentinel for this one check means adopting that platform. This tool reads the same terraform show -json file open-source Terraform and OpenTofu already produce, so it runs in any CI system, any pre-commit hook, or a browser, with no platform requirement.

Can this checker replace an existing Sentinel or OPA policy set entirely?

Only for this specific question. Sentinel and OPA/Conftest are general-purpose policy engines organizations use for cost limits, tagging standards, allowed regions, module version pins, and many rules beyond destructive changes — this tool checks exactly one thing, whether a replace or destroy lands on a resource type that holds data. Teams already invested in Sentinel or OPA for other policies can still run this tool as a fast, zero-configuration second opinion on that one question, or port its token-matching approach into their existing Rego or Sentinel policy.

What happens when this tool does not recognize a new resource type?

It is biased toward flagging rather than staying silent: the heuristic matches on tokens in the resource type name itself (database, disk, bucket, DNS, and so on), not a hand-maintained list of exact type names, so a provider's new resource type is caught automatically if its name carries one of those tokens. A hand-written Sentinel or Rego policy that enumerates exact type strings has the opposite failure mode — it stays silent on any type nobody added yet, which is the gap this tool's name-based matching is built to avoid.

Open the Terraform Plan Blast Radius Check against your own plan, or read why a replace destroys data.

No warranty. This free tool is informational only. It is not legal, security, compliance, or other professional advice, and a clean report is not a statement that an apply is safe -- only that nothing in the plan matched the patterns it checks. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The CLI and the browser page both read your plan file locally and make no network call. This page describes Sentinel, Terraform Cloud, Terraform Enterprise, OPA, Rego, and Conftest in general terms for comparison; it is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by HashiCorp, the Open Policy Agent project, Styra, or any of their trademark holders. Terraform and Sentinel are trademarks of HashiCorp.

Free and open source. If it helps you catch a destructive apply, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

why-terraform-replace-destroys-data.html.text:
← Back to Terraform Plan Blast Radius Check

Why a Terraform replace destroys data, and why the plan won't always say which attribute forced it

The mechanism, in one paragraph

Every attribute in a Terraform provider's schema can be marked ForceNew (the modern plugin framework calls the same thing RequiresReplace). The flag means one thing: the cloud API behind this resource offers no way to change this field on an existing object. So when that field's value moves, Terraform has exactly one route from the current state to your desired state — destroy the object and create a new one. It reports this as must be replaced, and it is not a bug or a provider mistake. It is the honest consequence of an API that has no update path for that field.

For a virtual machine, a replacement is an outage you can plan around. For a database, a disk, a bucket, a queue, or a KMS key, the new object is empty, and nothing in the plan puts the old contents back. The restore, if a restore is even possible, is a separate thing you do by hand afterwards — assuming a snapshot exists and assuming the retention window has not already expired.

Why the summary line cannot warn you

A plan ends with one line:

Plan: 3 to add, 1 to change, 2 to destroy.

A replacement is counted in both the add column and the destroy column. So a plan that recreates one production database and deletes one abandoned log group produces the same trailing line as a plan that creates two scratch resources and deletes two others. The information that separates them exists — it is in the -/+ resource "aws_db_instance" "primary" header hundreds of lines up, next to the # forces replacement comment — and it is in the part of the output that a reviewer skims, a CI log truncates, and a pull-request bot collapses behind a "show more" toggle.

This is a presentation problem, not a data problem. Terraform knows precisely which resources are being replaced and which attributes forced each one. It is simply not the thing it puts at the end.

The part that is hidden on purpose

There is a sharper version of this, and it is worth knowing because no amount of careful reading of the text output fixes it. An attribute a provider marked RequiresReplace whose own value did not change is folded into the (N unchanged attributes hidden) summary — so the plan tells you the resource must be replaced and does not show you the field responsible.

This was reported upstream as hashicorp/terraform#36097, "terraform plan hides unchanged forces replacement attributes", and closed as working as designed. The reporter's example was a TLS certificate being replaced because of ready_for_renewal, an attribute that never appeared anywhere in the plan output.

The structured plan does not hide it. terraform show -json emits, per resource change, a replace_paths array carrying the exact attribute paths that forced the replacement, regardless of whether their values changed — the field was added for precisely this reason, so that consumers of the format can determine which paths caused a replacement.

The three fields that answer the question

Everything this tool reports comes out of resource_changes[] in the structured plan:

FieldWhat it settles
change.actionsThe action, as an array. ["delete","create"] and ["create","delete"] are both replacements — the second is the create_before_destroy form, which avoids the gap in service but not the loss of anything stored on the old object.
change.replace_pathsThe attribute paths that forced the replacement, including the ones the text output hides.
action_reasonWhy this action rather than an update: replace_because_cannot_update (the ForceNew case), replace_because_tainted, replace_by_request (you passed -replace=), delete_because_no_resource_config, delete_because_count_index, and others. Terraform documents these as display hints whose set can change, and tells consumers to expect codes they do not recognise — so this tool prints an unknown code rather than dropping it.

A replacement can legitimately have no replace_paths at all: a tainted resource and an explicit -replace=ADDRESS are replaced for reasons that are not any attribute. In those cases action_reason is the whole answer, which is why the report shows both columns.

A "true deletion" is not the same as a destroy count

The destroy count in a plan includes the destroy half of every replacement. What a reviewer usually wants to know is narrower: what is going away and not coming back? That is a resource whose actions are exactly ["delete"] and which nothing else in the plan re-creates at the same address.

The qualifier matters. A create_before_destroy replacement of a deposed object arrives in the plan as two separate entries at the same address — one ["create"], and one ["delete"] carrying a deposed key. Counting that delete as a resource going away would be a false alarm on a perfectly ordinary rolling replacement, and a list that cries wolf is a list nobody reads by the third week.

Where prevent_destroy stops helping

lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } is the right backstop and you should use it on anything that holds data. It is not a substitute for reading the plan, for three reasons: it has to have been added to the resource in advance, so it does nothing for the resource somebody forgot; it fails the whole apply rather than telling you which attribute to change; and it says nothing at review time, which is the moment a replacement is cheapest to catch.

The gap is not hypothetical. GitLab's own infrastructure team published a corrective action — "Improve safety around Terraform destroy operations (disks)" — after an accidental deletion of three recently created Gitaly nodes cost roughly 30 minutes of data loss on each. The action they asked for is exactly the missing half: an apply should fail if multiple critical resources containing data (disks) are being deleted. That is a check on the plan, before the apply, on resources identified by what they hold.

What this is not

This is not a policy engine like Sentinel, OPA, or Conftest, and it is not a cost estimator. It writes no rules for you, evaluates no expressions, and makes no judgement about whether a change should be allowed — it reads exactly one file, the structured plan JSON you already have from your own terraform show -json, and reports what that file says is being destroyed and replaced. It makes no claim about your state file, your provider's source code, or whether a resource it does not flag is safe to lose.

Common questions

What is ForceNew and why does it destroy my data?

ForceNew is a flag a provider author sets on a schema attribute to say that the underlying cloud API offers no way to change that field on an existing object. When such an attribute changes, Terraform's only route to your desired state is to destroy the object and create a new one. For a virtual machine that is an outage; for a database, a disk, or a bucket it is the data as well, because the new object is empty and nothing in the plan restores it.

Why doesn't the plan always show the attribute that forced the replacement?

Because an attribute a provider marked RequiresReplace whose own value did not change is folded into the (N unchanged attributes hidden) summary, so the plan can say a resource must be replaced without showing which field caused it. This was reported upstream as hashicorp/terraform#36097 and closed as working as designed. The structured plan JSON does not hide it — change.replace_paths carries the exact attribute paths whether or not their values changed.

Isn't prevent_destroy enough?

It is the right backstop and it is not a substitute for reading the plan. prevent_destroy makes the apply fail rather than proceed, which is valuable, but it has to have been added to the resource in advance, it stops the whole apply rather than telling you what to change, and it does nothing for a resource somebody forgot to annotate. A public GitLab corrective action after an incident that lost roughly 30 minutes of data on three nodes asked for exactly the missing half: an apply should fail if multiple critical resources containing data are being deleted.

Why read the JSON plan instead of the text output?

Because the text output is designed for a human reading it top to bottom at the moment it is produced, and the two facts that matter most — which resources are replaced and why — are scattered through it and summarised at the end in columns that conflate a replacement with a creation and a deletion. The structured plan is the same information as data: one array of resource changes, each with an actions list, a replace_paths list, and an action_reason code. Anything can read it, including a CI gate that runs before the apply step.
